title: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
blurb: Classify chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia, and apply NICE NG133 on aspirin, labetalol, the 135/85 target, PlGF testing, timing of birth and postnatal care.
question: At 30 weeks, Leila's blood pressure is 148/96 on two readings. It was 118/72 at booking and her urine PCR is normal. What is her diagnosis and how should it be managed?

teach.h: Three conditions, one blood pressure cuff
teach.body: Formally (NICE NG133): chronic hypertension is present at booking or before 20 weeks, or she is already on treatment; gestational hypertension is new hypertension after 20 weeks without significant proteinuria; pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria or other maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction. In plain English: when did the high blood pressure start, and is anything else affected? Hypertension means 140/90 or more; severe means over 160 systolic or over 110 diastolic.

teach.caption: Organ dysfunction includes creatinine 90 micromol/L or more, raised transaminases, neurological signs (clonus, severe headache, scotomata), platelets under 150,000 and uteroplacental dysfunction such as fetal growth restriction.

First pregnancy, age 40+, interval over 10 years, BMI 35+, family history, multiple pregnancy
teach.caption: Aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth. For this use it must be prescribed.
NG133 1.3.8-1.3.10, 1.4.5, 1.5.6. Do not offer bed rest in hospital as a treatment for gestational hypertension (1.4.6).

teach.body: ACE inhibitors and ARBs carry an increased risk of congenital abnormalities: stop them if she becomes pregnant, preferably within 2 working days of notification, and offer an alternative. Thiazide diuretics may also increase risk. Women with chronic hypertension also get advice on weight, exercise, healthy eating and salt, and aspirin from 12 weeks.

items: Booking BP 118/72; now 148/96 twice; PCR normal; no symptoms. Leila has gestational hypertension.
The midwife refers her for a full assessment in secondary care by a clinician trained in hypertensive disorders (1.4.1).
She is offered labetalol, aiming for 135/85, with BP and urine checks once or twice a week and weekly bloods.
The midwife teaches her the warning symptoms: severe headache, visual problems, pain below the ribs, vomiting, sudden swelling.
Birth is not planned before 37 weeks unless BP reaches 160/110 or other indications arise.
Measure BP daily for the first 2 days and at least once between days 3 and 5 (chronic and gestational hypertension).
Stop methyldopa within 2 days of the birth and switch to an alternative.
Enalapril is first choice after birth, including when breastfeeding; nifedipine or amlodipine for women of Black African or Caribbean family origin.
Start treatment at 150/100 or more if untreated; reduce treatment if BP falls below 130/80.
GP or specialist review 2 weeks after birth if on treatment, and a medical review at 6 to 8 weeks.

teach.text: ACE inhibitors: stopped in pregnancy, but enalapril is the FIRST choice after birth, even when breastfeeding. And methyldopa is the third-line choice in pregnancy but is stopped within 2 days of the birth and replaced.

items: Chronic: before 20 weeks. Gestational: new after 20 weeks, no proteinuria. Pre-eclampsia: new after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or organ dysfunction.
Aspirin 75-150 mg from 12 weeks: one high-risk factor or more than one moderate factor.
Treat at 140/90; labetalol, then nifedipine, then methyldopa; target 135/85.
PlGF-based testing helps rule out pre-eclampsia from 20+0 to 36+6 weeks.
Pre-eclampsia from 37 weeks: initiate birth within 24-48 hours. After birth: enalapril first; stop methyldopa within 2 days.

summary: You can now classify the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, identify who needs aspirin, and apply NICE NG133 treatment thresholds, drug order and the 135/85 target. You can also plan monitoring, timing of birth and postnatal treatment.

A.q: At 28 weeks, a woman's BP is 146/94 on repeated readings. It was 112/70 at booking. Her urine PCR is normal and her bloods are normal. What is the diagnosis?
A.why: New hypertension presenting after 20 weeks without significant proteinuria is gestational hypertension (NG133).

whyNot.0: Chronic hypertension is present at booking or before 20 weeks; her booking BP was normal.
whyNot.2: Pre-eclampsia needs significant proteinuria or organ or uteroplacental dysfunction, which are absent.
whyNot.3: Repeated raised readings in clinic with a normal booking BP are treated as gestational hypertension, not dismissed.

A.q: Which antihypertensive does NICE NG133 recommend as first choice for a pregnant woman with gestational hypertension?
A.why: NG133 1.4.5: consider labetalol first; nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable; methyldopa if neither is suitable.

whyNot.0: Methyldopa is third choice, used if labetalol and nifedipine are not suitable.
whyNot.1: Nifedipine is second choice, for women in whom labetalol is not suitable.
whyNot.3: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are not used in pregnancy because of the risk of congenital abnormalities.

A.q: A woman with chronic hypertension is started on labetalol in pregnancy. What target blood pressure does NICE recommend?
A.why: NG133 1.3.9: when using medicines to treat hypertension in pregnancy, aim for 135/85 mmHg.

whyNot.0: 130/80 is the threshold below which postnatal treatment may be reduced, not the antenatal target.
whyNot.1: 140/90 is the threshold for starting treatment, not the target.
whyNot.2: 150/100 is the postnatal threshold for starting treatment in women not already treated.

B.q: A woman taking ramipril for hypertension finds she is 6 weeks pregnant. What does NICE NG133 advise?
options: Stop it within 2 working days and switch
Continue it until the booking scan
Continue it if BP is well controlled
B.why: NG133 1.3.3: stop ACE inhibitors or ARBs if she becomes pregnant, preferably within 2 working days of notification, and offer alternatives.

whyNot.1: Waiting until the scan prolongs exposure to a drug linked with congenital abnormalities.
whyNot.2: Dose reduction does not remove the risk; the drug should be stopped and replaced.
whyNot.3: Good control does not make an ACE inhibitor safe in pregnancy.

B.q: Between which gestations does NICE recommend PlGF-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia?
B.why: NG133 1.4.4: offer PlGF-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia in women with suspected pre-eclampsia between 20 weeks and 36 weeks 6 days.

whyNot.0: Pre-eclampsia is a diagnosis after 20 weeks; testing does not start at 12 weeks.
whyNot.2: 24+0 weeks is too late a start and 37 weeks is beyond the recommended window.
whyNot.3: 28+0 to 40+0 does not match the NICE window.

B.q: A woman with pre-eclampsia is now 37+3 weeks. Her BP is controlled and bloods are stable. What does NICE advise about timing of birth?
B.why: NG133 table 3: from 37 weeks in pre-eclampsia, initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours.

whyNot.0: Expectant care to 40 weeks is not recommended for pre-eclampsia after 37 weeks.
whyNot.1: Waiting until 39 weeks exceeds the 24 to 48 hour window.
whyNot.3: Mode of birth is chosen by circumstance and preference; NICE does not mandate urgent caesarean.

C.q: Bisi had chronic hypertension treated with methyldopa during pregnancy. She gave birth yesterday and is breastfeeding. What should happen to her methyldopa?
options: Continue it until she stops feeding
C.why: NG133 1.3.19: stop methyldopa within 2 days after the birth and change to an alternative antihypertensive.

whyNot.0: NICE advises stopping methyldopa within 2 days, not continuing for weeks.
whyNot.1: Increasing the dose goes against the advice to stop it after the birth.
whyNot.2: Breastfeeding does not change the advice to stop methyldopa within 2 days.

C.q: Nicola, who is of White British family origin, had pre-eclampsia and needs antihypertensive treatment after the birth. She is breastfeeding. Which drug is first choice?
C.why: NG133 1.9.4: offer enalapril to treat hypertension after birth, including in women who are breastfeeding.

whyNot.1: Methyldopa should be stopped within 2 days of birth and is not a postnatal first choice.
whyNot.2: ARBs such as losartan should be avoided when breastfeeding.
whyNot.3: Diuretics should be avoided in women who are breastfeeding.

C.q: At 34 weeks, Ruth has gestational hypertension with BP 148/96, normal bloods and no symptoms. Which plan follows NICE NG133?
options: Admit for bed rest until birth
Plan induction of labour at 35 weeks
C.why: NG133 table 1: do not routinely admit; offer treatment if BP stays above 140/90 (labetalol first), with BP checks once or twice a week.

whyNot.0: NG133 1.4.6: do not offer bed rest in hospital for gestational hypertension, and admission is not routine below 160/110.
whyNot.2: Planned birth before 37 weeks is not offered when BP is below 160/110 without other indications.
whyNot.3: Treatment is offered when BP remains above 140/90, not delayed until severe.

reteach.title: When did it start, and what else is affected?
reteach.question: Two questions sort almost every hypertensive woman: when did the raised blood pressure begin, and is there protein in the urine or any organ affected?

blocks.body: Raised before 20 weeks: chronic. New after 20 weeks on its own: gestational. New after 20 weeks with protein or organ trouble (kidneys, liver, brain, blood, placenta): pre-eclampsia. Whatever the label, treat at 140/90 with labetalol first and aim for 135/85. Pre-eclampsia needs closer watching, and from 37 weeks the baby should be born within 24 to 48 hours.

blocks.text: Treat at 140/90, aim for 135/85. The 150/100 figure is the threshold for starting treatment AFTER the birth in women not already on treatment.

explain.body: Chronic: present at booking, before 20 weeks, or already treated. Gestational: new after 20 weeks without significant proteinuria. Pre-eclampsia: new after 20 weeks with PCR 30 mg/mmol+, ACR 8 mg/mmol+ or organ or uteroplacental dysfunction (NG133).

test.q: A woman whose BP was 150/95 at her 9-week booking appointment is now 24 weeks pregnant. Which disorder does she have?
test.why: Hypertension present at booking or before 20 weeks is chronic hypertension (NG133).

whyNot.0: Gestational hypertension is new hypertension after 20 weeks.
whyNot.1: Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or organ dysfunction.
whyNot.3: HELLP is a severe form of pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets, not described here.

explain.body: Aspirin 75-150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth if one high-risk factor (previous hypertensive pregnancy, CKD, autoimmune disease, diabetes, chronic hypertension) or more than one moderate factor (first pregnancy, 40+, interval over 10 years, BMI 35+, family history, multiple pregnancy).

test.q: Which woman should be advised to take aspirin from 12 weeks to reduce her risk of pre-eclampsia?
options: Age 41, second baby, no other factors
test.why: Type 1 diabetes is a high-risk factor; one high-risk factor is enough for aspirin (NG133 1.1.2).

whyNot.0: She has no high-risk factors and no moderate factors.
whyNot.1: Age 40 or over is a single moderate factor; more than one moderate factor is needed.
whyNot.2: First pregnancy is a single moderate factor; more than one is needed.

explain.body: Offer treatment at sustained 140/90 or more. Labetalol first, nifedipine if unsuitable, methyldopa if both unsuitable. Target 135/85. Stop ACE inhibitors and ARBs within 2 working days of pregnancy notification. No hospital bed rest for gestational hypertension.

test.q: A woman with pre-eclampsia has asthma, so labetalol is unsuitable. Which antihypertensive should be offered next?
test.why: NG133 1.5.6: offer nifedipine for women in whom labetalol is not suitable, and methyldopa if neither is suitable.

whyNot.1: Methyldopa is used if both labetalol and nifedipine are unsuitable.
whyNot.2: Atenolol is not an NG133 choice in pregnancy; NICE lists it only as a postnatal add-on or swap (1.9.6).
whyNot.3: ACE inhibitors are not used in pregnancy.

explain.body: Pre-eclampsia: before 37 weeks continue surveillance unless indications; from 37 weeks initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours. Chronic or gestational with BP under 160/110: no planned birth before 37 weeks without other indications. After birth: enalapril first; stop methyldopa within 2 days; BP daily for 2 days and once between days 3 and 5.

test.q: After the birth, a woman with gestational hypertension who did not need antenatal medicines has BP 152/102. What does NICE advise?
options: Advise rest and recheck next week
test.why: NG133 1.4.13: for women with gestational hypertension not on treatment, start antihypertensive treatment after birth if BP is 150/100 or higher.

whyNot.0: Waiting 6 weeks leaves BP above the treatment threshold untreated.
whyNot.2: Aspirin is for preventing pre-eclampsia antenatally; it does not treat postnatal hypertension.
whyNot.3: BP at or above 150/100 after birth should be treated, not simply rechecked later.
